title: Storytelling with Data
author: Cole Nussbaumer Knaflic
summary: Knaflic shows how to turn analysis into a message an audience actually understands. She covers choosing the right chart for the question, stripping out clutter that competes for attention, and using colour and position to direct the eye to what matters. For my Power BI work, the lesson is to start from the one insight a stakeholder needs and design the visual around it.
takeaway: Good analysis is not enough; the insight must also be communicated clearly.

title: Emotional Intelligence
author: Daniel Goleman
summary: Goleman argues that self-awareness, self-management, motivation, empathy and relationship skills shape success as much as intellect does. For an analyst, these skills decide whether findings land: reading a stakeholder's concerns, staying composed when numbers are challenged, and delivering difficult news constructively. The book reframes communication, teamwork and leadership as abilities that can be practised and improved, not fixed personality traits.
takeaway: Professional effectiveness depends not only on technical ability but also on understanding and managing emotions.

title: Data Science for Business
author: Foster Provost & Tom Fawcett
summary: Provost and Fawcett explain core data science ideas through business problems rather than code: framing a question as a prediction task, building and evaluating models, avoiding overfitting, and judging results by the value they create. It provides a shared vocabulary for working with data scientists and a useful discipline: ask which decision a model will improve before building anything.
takeaway: The purpose of data science is not simply to build models; it is to solve meaningful business problems.

title: Thinking, Fast and Slow
author: Daniel Kahneman
summary: Kahneman describes two modes of thinking: a fast, intuitive system that jumps to conclusions, and a slower, deliberate one that checks the work. Through biases such as anchoring, availability and overconfidence, he shows how easily judgment drifts. For anyone presenting data, it is a reminder that good reporting should slow people down at the right moments and make the evidence hard to ignore.
takeaway: Better decisions require recognizing when intuition may be misleading and when deliberate analysis is necessary.

title: Start with Why
author: Simon Sinek
summary: Sinek's Golden Circle argues that leaders and organisations inspire action when they communicate why they do something before explaining how and what. Starting with purpose builds trust and lasting loyalty rather than one-off compliance. Applied to analytics, it means clarifying the decision and the purpose behind a reporting request before discussing metrics, tools or visuals.
takeaway: People connect more strongly with a clear purpose than with a list of features or actions.

title: Atomic Habits
author: James Clear
summary: Clear explains how small, repeatable improvements compound into major results. He focuses on building systems instead of chasing goals, tying habits to the identity you want to build, and designing your environment so good behaviours are obvious and easy to repeat. The approach is especially practical for continuous learning, such as building SQL, Power BI and certification skills alongside full-time work.
takeaway: Small improvements repeated consistently can produce significant long-term change.

title: A Guide to the Business Analysis Body of Knowledge (BABOK Guide)
author: International Institute of Business Analysis (IIBA)
summary: The BABOK Guide is the recognised framework for business analysis practice. It organises the work into knowledge areas: elicitation and collaboration, stakeholder engagement, strategy analysis, requirements analysis and design, and solution evaluation. For a modern analyst working between business teams, data, technology and decision-makers, it offers a shared structure for turning vague needs into clear, testable requirements.
takeaway: Effective business analysis connects business needs with practical, measurable solutions.

title: The Psychology of Money
author: Morgan Housel
summary: Housel shows that financial outcomes depend less on technical knowledge than on behaviour: personal experience, emotion, patience and how we perceive risk. Through short, memorable stories he explains compounding, leaving room for error and knowing when enough is enough. Alongside an accounting background, it is a reminder that people rarely act on numbers alone, which matters whenever analysis meets real decisions.
takeaway: Financial decisions are often driven more by behavior and psychology than by mathematical knowledge.

title: How to Become a Data Analyst
author: Annie Nelson
summary: Drawing on her own career change, Nelson lays out a practical, low-cost roadmap into data analytics: the core tools such as SQL, spreadsheets and visualisation software, building a portfolio, networking, and navigating the job search. Her emphasis on pairing technical skills with business understanding reflects how I see the analyst role: the value lies in solving real problems, not simply in using tools.
takeaway: Becoming a strong data analyst requires combining technical skills with the ability to understand and solve business problems.

title: The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People
author: Stephen R. Covey
summary: Covey presents a principle-based framework for personal and interpersonal effectiveness: be proactive, begin with the end in mind, put first things first, think win-win, seek first to understand, synergise, and keep renewing yourself. The habits translate directly to analytics work, from prioritising the requests that matter most to listening carefully before proposing a dashboard or solution.
takeaway: Long-term effectiveness comes from principles, priorities, relationships, and consistent personal discipline.
